extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, funders, and other stakeholders interested in peer review reform
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the quality, fairness, reliability, and processes of scholarly peer review and assessing proposed interventions (e.g., open review, training, incentives, preprints, editorial procedures). The paper surveys problems and weighs pros/cons of solutions across disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is intended to support scientific integrity, correct errors, and democratize decisions about publication and funding, but review quality is questioned—reviews often provide insufficient scrutiny, miss major manuscript errors, and contribute to irreproducibility and retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible remedies include recruiting more qualified reviewers, reviewer training, reproducibility checklists, publishing review histories, open/signed reviews, use of specialist reviewers (e.g., statisticians), and editorial oversight to focus on higher-level logical flaws rather than minor details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer conflicts of interest and self-serving behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Some reviewers engage in self-serving behaviors: obstructing publication of articles unfavorable to them, or self-appropriating ideas from manuscripts seen during review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency measures (publishing review histories, signed reviews) can help identify conflicts of interest; editorial vigilance and COI policies are needed to deter and detect such behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias across authors, topics, methods, institutions, geography, and demographics
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can be biased for or against authors, topics, methods, groups, institutions, countries, and demographic characteristics, accumulating into large disparities (e.g., prestige bias, homophily).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations discussed include double-blind review, publishing reviews, signed reviews combined with transparency, reviewer training, and broader/diversified reviewer recruitment; empirical results are mixed and context-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability / inter-reviewer agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: The reliability of peer review is low: meta-analyses report low average correlations between reviewers (e.g., 0.34), and reviewers frequently disagree, making outcomes unpredictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options to increase reliability include larger reviewer samples with averaged ratings, focusing revisions on points where reviewers agree or where reviewers have specific expertise, introducing reproducibility checklists, and conducting empirical randomized trials to test interventions. Editors should synthesize and prioritize reviewer points to reduce contradictory revision cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed and timeliness of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is often slow (months to years), which can be mismatched with rapid research advances and real-world decision timelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preprints and preprint peer review can speed dissemination; crowdsourced review processes, improved reviewer recruitment, compensation/incentives, and editorial triage (clear desk rejection criteria and focused editorial summaries) are proposed to reduce delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer availability, incentives, and recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: It is increasingly difficult to recruit reviewers; reviewing is generally uncompensated and often not rewarded in career advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested remedies include monetary compensation, recognition platforms (Publons), publishing peer reviews, reviewer credit services (e.g., Reviewer Credit), and formal verification of reviewing activity; feasibility varies by journal resources and equity concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open and transparent peer review (transparent review and signed reviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review includes (1) publishing peer review histories (editorial letters, reviewer comments, author responses) and (2) signed reviews (revealing reviewer identities). Implementations vary across journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency can increase accountability, enable metaresearch, and clarify editorial decisions, but signed reviews may reduce criticalness, risk retaliation for less-privileged reviewers, and shift incentives (e.g., reviewers signing positive reviews to curry favor). Hybrid and optional models exist; effects are context-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing peer reviews and review histories
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing reviews (and editorial correspondence) allows comparison of review quality across journals and makes reviewer contributions citable and visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits include increased incentives and opportunities for metaresearch; downsides include potential reduction in critical feedback and workforce reluctance if signing is mandatory. Practices vary (some journals publish histories for accepted papers only).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprint peer review and community-organized review
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints enable rapid dissemination and broader community feedback but lack formal peer review; community initiatives (e.g., Peer Community In*, PREreview) offer organized review and recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preprints can reduce publication bias and speed uptake, but many preprints receive no feedback and risk spreading unchecked errors or misinformation (notably in health contexts). Solutions include dedicated community review, AI-assisted triage with human validation, and services that link preprint reviews to journal acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limits of AI in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: AI can assist in scaling reviews (analytical checks, code checks, grammar), but accuracy and utility require careful validation and human oversight; risks of misuse and poor performance exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI may be valuable for routine checks but should not replace expert human judgment; its role must be empirically validated and integrated with human review processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility checklists and badges
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals and conferences add reproducibility checklists at submission (items on experimental design, statistical evaluation, model calibration) and run reproducibility projects awarding badges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklists appear to improve code/data sharing in some domains but evidence for improving review quality is limited; their effectiveness likely varies by field and implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer training (existence and effectiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal systematic reviewer training is limited; much training is informal. While many reviewers want training, randomized trials show limited evidence of effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training could improve review quality but is challenging to scale; targeted training for compensated reviewer pools (e.g., grant panels) might be more feasible; communicate clear journal expectations to reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted/specialized reviewing (fractionated reviewer roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: As science becomes more specialized, expecting reviewers to assess an entire manuscript is increasingly burdensome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems can ask reviewers to judge only facets within their expertise (e.g., statistics, methods), recruit specialists (statistical experts), and highlight which specialization each reviewer covered (e.g., via signed reviews or editorial notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment breadth and diversity of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Expanding reviewer pools (geographically and demographically) could relieve reviewer shortages and reduce bias; some regions supply disproportionate manuscripts relative to reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategies include broader outreach, crowdsourcing platforms (PREreview), automated reviewer recommendation algorithms, and reducing barriers for global participation; care needed to motivate and support new reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated reviewer recommendation systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal management systems use algorithms/machine learning to recommend candidate reviewers to editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated recommendations can broaden reviewer pools and reduce invitation load, but validity and relevance of algorithmic suggestions must be assessed and cannot be taken for granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial process transparency and decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial decision-making (including desk rejections and how editors weigh reviews) is often opaque; practices vary widely across editors and disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency options include publishing editorial statistics and correspondence, requiring editorial summaries, using interactive review platforms (e.g., Frontiers, OpenReview), and standardizing elements of the decision process to increase fairness and consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchical logical assessment by editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors could apply a semistructured hierarchical assessment: prioritize high-level questions (logic of design, answerability) before lower-level issues (sample size, minor discussion points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: reconcile conflicting reviews, shorten wait times, clarify revision trajectories, and make editorial decisions more uniform. Drawbacks: requires skilled editors, increases editor workload, and may not capture subjective impact judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desk rejection guidelines and standardization
rubrics_metrics.description: Many journals desk-reject a large portion of submissions for lack of relevance or competitiveness; lack of standardized practices can be unfair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing sensible and practical desk-rejection guidelines (transparency about criteria and statistics) can improve fairness; editorial portals and summaries can clarify reasons for rejection and speed decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focusing revisions on points of reviewer agreement and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Given reviewer disagreement, editors should emphasize where reviewers agree or where a reviewer has explicit expertise (e.g., statistical comments) rather than passing all reviews verbatim to authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach can increase the efficiency and productivity of revision cycles and reduce authors' overfitting to idiosyncratic reviewer preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evaluation of peer review interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a lack of rigorous evidence about which peer review reforms work; randomized trials and empirical tests are needed but can be difficult to implement ethically and practically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for more empirical studies and randomized evaluations of interventions (e.g., signed reviews, training, checklists) and creation of international best-practice research networks to build the evidence base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity considerations and impacts on less-privileged reviewers/authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Interventions (e.g., signed reviews, compensation) may have unequal effects: fear of retaliation can silence early-career or marginalized reviewers, and resource-intensive reforms may privilege wealthy publishers and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should consider distributional impacts, support equitable participation (including LMIC reviewers), and avoid amplifying existing privileges; include conceptual analysis and clearly defined objectives before implementing reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predatory journals and safeguards against lax review
rubrics_metrics.description: Predatory journals with lax or nonexistent peer review publish for a fee, worsening signal-to-noise and enabling questionable research dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent editorial processes, publishing review histories, and community-organized review (PCI) can help distinguish reputable outlets; raising awareness and institutional recognition policies may reduce incentives to publish in predatory venues.
